name: Nitin Saxena
milestone_by_age_26: Co-discovered the AKS primality test in 2002 as an undergraduate at IIT Kanpur, the first deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for primality testing, published in Annals of Mathematics in 2004.
early_history_summary: Saxena was an undergraduate at IIT Kanpur studying computer science when he and batchmate Neeraj Kayal, under professor Manindra Agrawal, developed the AKS primality test as part of their joint B.Tech. thesis. Both had represented India at the 1997 International Mathematical Olympiad. The paper 'PRIMES is in P' was posted online in 2002 and published in Annals of Mathematics in 2004, attracting worldwide attention including a New York Times article.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Saxena attended Boys' High School and College in Allahabad (Prayagraj), India.
primary_early_advantage_tags: IIT Kanpur, IMO 1997, Manindra Agrawal mentorship, Neeraj Kayal collaboration
evidence_summary: Saxena was a B.Tech. student at IIT Kanpur when he co-discovered the AKS primality test at age 21 with his batchmate Neeraj Kayal and professor Manindra Agrawal. Both students had been IMO participants, suggesting early mathematical training. The work was part of their undergraduate thesis and was published in Annals of Mathematics, one of the most prestigious journals in mathematics. The trio later won the Gödel Prize (2006) and Fulkerson Prize (2006) for this work. Saxena's family background is not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Subhash Khot
milestone_by_age_26: Formulated the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC) in 2001 as a PhD student at Princeton, which became one of the most influential ideas in theoretical computer science and earned him the Rolf Nevanlinna Prize and MacArthur Fellowship.
early_history_summary: Khot was born in Ichalkaranji, Maharashtra, India, and completed his B.Tech. at IIT Bombay in 1999. He then went to Princeton for his PhD under Sanjeev Arora, where he breezed through department prerequisites in three months. In the summer of 2001, while visiting relatives in India, he had the key insight that became the Unique Games Conjecture. He completed his PhD in 2003 and the UGC went on to become one of the most influential ideas in computational complexity theory.

He completed his PhD in 2003 at age 25 and went on to win the Waterman Award (2010), Nevanlinna Prize (2014), and MacArthur Fellowship (2016). Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Maryam Mirzakhani

She published papers as an undergraduate at Sharif University of Technology before moving to Harvard for her PhD under Curtis McMullen.

early_history_summary: Ngwenya was born in South Africa and enrolled for a BA in sociology and geography at Wits in 2015, completing it in 2017. She then pursued a BSc honors in geography with a focus on sustainability science. Her honors research on public participation in carbon capture and storage was so exceptional that her supervisor, Professor Danny Simatele, recommended she skip the master's and go directly to a PhD. She completed her PhD in three years, graduating at 25 in 2022.
